summary: Extends the PPP IP Control Protocol so that primary and secondary DNS server addresses and NetBIOS name server addresses can be negotiated when a link comes up. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When a dial-up link starts, the other end can tell your computer which phone books to use.

subtitle: Extend PPP to negotiate DNS and NetBIOS name server addresses when a dial-up link comes up.

tldr.problem: When a computer dials up to an ISP using PPP, it needs to know which DNS servers to use for name resolution, but standard PPP provides no way to negotiate this automatically.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC extends PPP's IP Control Protocol (IPCP) with four new configuration options that allow the remote peer to provide the addresses of primary and secondary DNS servers and NetBIOS name servers during the PPP handshake.
tldr.outcome: Dial-up clients can now receive name server addresses automatically as part of link negotiation, eliminating the need for manual configuration.

today: RFC 1877 is an Informational standard for automatic name server configuration on PPP dial-up links. It became widely implemented as ISPs adopted it to simplify the dial-up experience. Modern broadband and VPN connections also use similar automatic configuration mechanisms based on this model.

sections.title: Name Server Addresses over PPP
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) is the standard protocol for dial-up and other point-to-point connections. PPP uses Network Control Protocols (NCPs) to set up different network layers: one NCP handles IP configuration. This RFC extends the IP Control Protocol (IPCP) to allow negotiation of Domain Name System (DNS) server addresses and NetBIOS Name Server (NBNS) addresses.

Without this extension, a dial-up client has no way to learn which DNS servers the ISP uses, and must either have them pre-configured or ask the user to enter them manually. This RFC enables automatic discovery during the PPP handshake, so clients can resolve domain names immediately after connecting.
sections.eli5: PPP is the protocol dial-up modems use to talk to ISPs. This RFC adds a way for the ISP to tell your computer which name servers to use, instead of you having to type them in yourself.

sections.title: Four New Configuration Options
sections.content:
This RFC defines four new IPCP configuration options, numbered 129 through 132. Each option carries a single Internet address (four octets) and specifies what role it plays:

Type 129: Primary DNS Server Address—The primary DNS server the local peer should use for name resolution. Type 130: Primary NBNS Server Address—The primary NetBIOS Name Server, used on Windows networks for computer name resolution. Type 131: Secondary DNS Server Address—A secondary DNS server for fallback if the primary is unavailable. Type 132: Secondary NBNS Server Address—A secondary NBNS server.

All four options have identical format and behavior by design, matching the existing IPCP option 3 (IP-Address) for implementation simplicity. Primary and secondary servers are negotiated independently, and when both are present, the primary should be tried first.
sections.eli5: There are four new types of information you can ask for: which DNS server to use first, which to use as backup, and the same two things for Windows network names.

sections.title: Configuration Option Format
sections.content:
Each option follows a simple format: one byte for the Type (129, 130, 131, or 132), one byte for the Length (always 6, meaning one byte type plus one byte length plus four bytes of address), and four octets containing the IP address in network byte order.

The negotiation works as follows: the client sends a Configuration-Request with the desired option values. If the client sends zero in all four address octets (0.0.0.0), it is explicitly requesting that the peer provide the correct address in a Configuration-Nak response. The server responds with either an acknowledgment if the values are acceptable, or a Configuration-Nak containing the values the server wants the client to use. This is the standard IPCP negotiation mechanism: the client makes a suggestion, and the server either accepts it or provides the correct answer.
sections.eli5: The format is tiny: one byte says what kind of information it is, another byte says how big it is, and four bytes are the address. When the computer asks for a name server address, the ISP sends back the real one in a special message.

sections.title: Negotiation Process
sections.content:
When a PPP link comes up, both peers run IPCP to negotiate IP parameters. As part of this negotiation, the client can include one or more of the four name server options in its Configuration-Request message. The client typically does not know the correct server addresses yet, so it sends zeros (0.0.0.0) to request that the server provide them.

The server receives the Configuration-Request, sees the zero addresses, and responds with a Configuration-Nak message containing the actual server addresses it wants the client to use. Alternatively, the server can Ack the request, meaning it approves of the values (usually zeros) in the request. The client then adopts the addresses from the server's Nak or Ack response.

Both primary and secondary addresses are negotiated independently, so a client might request the primary DNS server separately from the secondary, or request DNS servers but not NBNS servers. The negotiation follows the standard IPCP configure-request/configure-ack/configure-nak flow, making implementation straightforward for systems that already support IPCP.
sections.eli5: The client asks for name servers by sending zeros. The ISP responds with the real addresses. The client uses whatever the ISP sends.

sections.title: Practical Impact and Design Rationale
sections.content:
This RFC eliminates a major pain point in dial-up configuration. Before this standard, ISPs had to provide users with an installer script or documentation listing the DNS servers to manually enter into their system settings. This RFC enables automatic discovery.

The design is intentionally simple and reuses the format of existing IPCP options to minimize implementation burden on vendors already supporting IPCP. The four options (primary and secondary, DNS and NBNS) cover the main name resolution needs of 1990s networks. DNS servers handle Internet domain names; NBNS handles NetBIOS names used on Windows networks for computer discovery and sharing.

The RFC is Informational rather than Standards Track, reflecting that it is a practical extension to PPP that implementations were already experimenting with. The lack of a mandatory-to-implement requirement means vendors can omit these options if their target market does not need them, though most PPP implementations adopted them.
sections.eli5: This lets ISPs configure computers automatically instead of making users type in addresses. It's designed to be easy to add to existing software. It handles two kinds of name servers: the Internet kind and the Windows network kind.
